source.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
source.authors: W. Fedus; Barret Zoph; Noam Shazeer

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether improved pretraining loss predicts downstream performance in sparse Switch models, extending the question to a different architecture and downstream settings. It does not test the power-law or compute-optimal-allocation claims.
record.gate_note: The paper measures negative log perplexity while scaling the number of experts, but does not fit or test power laws, extrapolate from small runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Those results are not rows for V1–V3. Kaplan et al.'s scaling-law findings are cited, not reproduced. Downstream task scores and the paper's pretraining-to-downstream comparisons bear on V6 and are recorded below.
record.test_reason: Appendix E compares C4 pretraining negative log perplexity with SuperGLUE and TriviaQA for dense and sparse (Switch) models. Table 5 reports downstream scores across dense and parameter-scaled models. Both bear on V6 in a new setting: sparse MoE models. The paper fits no power law, does no extrapolation and runs no compute-optimal sweep. Its loss-versus-expert-count curves (Fig. 4) scale parameters at fixed FLOPs per token without a fit, so they are not V1 evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find a consistent correlation: better C4 pretraining gives better downstream results for both dense and Switch models. At fixed perplexity the families perform similarly at small-to-medium scale. At the largest scale, Switch underperforms dense on SuperGLUE but may follow a better relation on TriviaQA. They call the evidence preliminary and say further statistics are needed. They call Switch-C vs Switch-XXL on SQuAD an anomaly, suggesting a poorly understood dependence on FLOPs per token and parameters.
record.recipe_differences: Uses sparsely activated Switch/Mixture-of-Experts Transformers and compares pretraining and downstream outcomes; it does not reproduce Kaplan's dense-model scaling-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream relationship varies by task and model family: dense models can outperform Switch models at fixed upstream perplexity on SuperGLUE in the large-scale regime, while Switch models may do better on TriviaQA. Authors also describe dependence on FLOPs per token, parameters, regularization, load balancing, and fine-tuning hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed FLOPs per token, C4 test loss falls consistently as sparse parameter count rises by doubling experts (223M to 14.7B; Fig. 4 left). Returns diminish (Sec. 5), and larger models are more sample-efficient. Switch-C (1.6T params, fewer FLOPs) has worse perplexity than Switch-XXL (395B) (Table 9). So parameters alone do not set loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining loss improves steadily with expert (sparse) parameter count at fixed per-token compute, with diminishing returns. Parameter count and FLOPs per token act as separate scaling axes.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the downstream scores or pretraining-to-downstream associations. The association evidence is presented in plots without reported correlation statistics; the authors note that further statistics would be needed to confirm the observations. The paper does not fit power laws or test extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: None of the Table 5 downstream score rows or relevant Appendix E/Future Work results were left out. Other reported pretraining scaling scores are excluded because the paper does not test a power-law form, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute. Fig. 4 plots loss against sparse parameter count at fixed FLOPs, with no fit.
No controlled shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Multilingual and fine-tuning results are reported only as speedups and gains, not as a power-law form.

No functional form or correlation statistic is fitted. There is no prediction of large-model downstream scores from small models, and no uncertainty. Only two tasks are used for the loss–downstream plots.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Switch-XXL has state-of-the-art C4 perplexity but SuperGLUE test 87.5 vs 89.3 for T5-XXL. Upstream gains do not translate to downstream.
C4 negative log perplexity at 250k/500k steps for T5 and Switch models. Needed to link Table 5 and future-squad-c downstream scores to pretraining loss.

record.verdict_notes: Table 5 rows chained models in table order (T5-Base → Switch-Base → T5-Large → Switch-Large), mixing two axes. Correct comparisons: Switch vs FLOP-matched T5 (parameter scaling) and T5-Large vs T5-Base (dense scaling). T5-Base rows are baselines only. Appendix E evidence is figure-only and has no correlation statistics.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test of loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of predictions from power laws fitted on small runs.
No fixed-compute sweep identifying optimal parameter and token counts or their growth rates.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Includes language pretraining, fine-tuning, and multilingual training, but does not test whether the claimed power-law form carries over to these regimes or other modalities.

Tests relations between upstream pretraining quality and selected downstream tasks, and reports downstream scores across several model sizes. It does not establish general predictability across tasks or training setups.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices, and does not test systematic departures from power laws.

relationships.condition: Dense and Switch models at small-to-medium scale; most Table 5 tasks
relationships.reason: Authors report a consistent correlation between C4 perplexity and SuperGLUE/TriviaQA for both families (appE-sg-dense, appE-trivia-dense, appE-trivia-switch). GLUE, SQuAD, SuperGLUE, Winogrande, XSum, ANLI and the closed-book QA tasks rise from T5-Base to T5-Large and from each T5 to its Switch counterpart (tab5-*-sb, tab5-*-t5l, tab5-*-sl for those tasks).
relationships.display_finding: C4 perplexity correlated consistently with SuperGLUE and TriviaQA performance, while the listed downstream tasks improved from T5-Base to T5-Large and from each T5 model to its Switch counterpart.

relationships.condition: Largest models; architecture family (sparse vs dense)
relationships.reason: At a given perplexity, dense beats Switch on SuperGLUE at large scale, while Switch beats dense on TriviaQA (appE-sg-switch, appE-trivia-switch). So the loss-to-downstream map depends on architecture and task. Switch-C scores below Switch-XXL on SQuAD despite similar perplexity and 4x the parameters (future-squad-c).
relationships.display_finding: At comparable perplexity, dense models outperform Switch on SuperGLUE while Switch wins on TriviaQA; Switch-C also trails Switch-XXL on SQuAD despite fourfold more parameters and similar perplexity.

relationships.reason: Switch-Large scores 66.0 vs 68.8 for T5-Large despite its gains elsewhere and better pretraining loss (tab5-arce-sl). ARC Easy otherwise improves with scale (tab5-arce-sb, tab5-arce-t5l).
relationships.display_finding: Switch-Large scores 66.0 versus T5-Large's 68.8 despite better pretraining loss, although ARC Easy otherwise improves with scale.

relationships.condition: ARC Challenge, all Table 5 scaling steps
relationships.reason: No scaling step improves ARC Challenge: T5-Base 35.5, T5-Large 35.5, Switch-Large 35.5, and Switch-Base drops to 32.8 (tab5-arcc-t5l, tab5-arcc-sl, tab5-arcc-sb).
relationships.display_finding: T5-Base, T5-Large and Switch-Large each scored 35.5, while Switch-Base scored 32.8, yielding no improvement across the tested scaling steps.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: ARC Easy, ARC Challenge, and large-scale SuperGLUE/SQuAD comparisons
reader_labels.reason: The gains are not uniform: Switch-Large is below T5-Large on ARC Easy, ARC Challenge does not improve over T5-Large, the authors report weak upstream-to-SuperGLUE translation for the largest Switch models, and Switch-C scores below Switch-XXL on SQuAD despite similar perplexity; see tab5-arce-sl, tab5-arcc-sb, tab5-arcc-sl, appE-sg-switch, future-squad-c, and sec56-squad-xxl.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported T5-Large score is below Switch-Base, so this task does not show a simple monotonic increase in the presented model ordering; see tab5-trivia-sb and tab5-trivia-t5l.
